# Working on Caroline

Caroline is a single-user, self-hosted assistant. It pulls work from GitHub, Gmail and Google
Calendar into one lightweight system, keeps the inbox sorted with an LLM, and proposes a daily
plan sized to the free time the calendar actually leaves. One Node process, one SQLite file, no
accounts and no multi-tenancy. [docs/specs/00-overview.md](docs/specs/00-overview.md) has the
architecture.

Node 24 or later, ESM, TypeScript in strict mode. Fastify 5 serves the JSON API and the built
SPA from the same process; the client is React 19 with Vite, Tailwind and shadcn/ui; storage is
SQLite through the built-in `node:sqlite`; tests are vitest with Testing Library.

`src/` is organised by subsystem, one directory each: `server/` (app, routes, schemas),
`domain/` (pure logic, no IO), `db/` (connection, migrations, repositories), `actions/` (what
the routes and the chat tools both do), `connectors/` (GitHub, Gmail, Calendar and the shared
sync engine), `llm/` (provider interface, adapters, prompts), `chat/` (tool registry, turn loop,
undo), `mcp/` (the external tool surface), `jobs/` (scheduler, classify, plan, purge), `auth/`,
`config/` and `cli/`. The client is in `web/`, the published site generator in `site/`.
Everything but the client is tested from `test/`, laid out by subsystem; the client's own tests
sit beside the code in `web/`, and there is no `test/web/`. `vitest.config.ts` runs the two as
separate projects, `node` for the first and `jsdom` for the second.

## Specs are the source of truth

Code is the byproduct. If an implementation and a spec disagree, one of them is a defect: decide
which, and fix that one. The specs live in [docs/specs](docs/specs/README.md), one per
subsystem, and its README is the reading order.

**Order of operations is spec, then docs, then code.** The natural default is to write the code
first and backfill the spec, which inverts it. If implementing reveals the spec is wrong, the
spec changes first, in the same commit.

## Acceptance criteria are appended, never renumbered

The code and the suite cite criteria by number, in comments and in test names, so inserting one
in the middle silently repoints every citation after it at a criterion it was not written about.
A new criterion goes at the end with the next free number, even where it would read better
beside the one it belongs with. One that is no longer wanted is left in place and said to be
superseded, not removed. Extending a criterion in place is fine, because its number still points
at the same contract. [docs/specs/README.md](docs/specs/README.md#conventions) is the full
statement.

## Which documents move with a behaviour change

- [docs/using.md](docs/using.md) has a table, under "What to say, and what happens", of what the
  chat surface can do and which tool answers each request. A change to a tool's name, arguments
  or answer leaves that table wrong.
- [docs/content-policy.md](docs/content-policy.md) is what leaves the machine and what stays on
  it, at each of the four content levels, with a payload shown at each.
- [README.md](README.md) is the shorter version of both, plus the reference table of
  configuration and environment variables.
- [docs/plan.md](docs/plan.md) records the milestone order and what each one proved, appended
  to as each milestone lands rather than rewritten.

[docs/README.md](docs/README.md) is the index of the rest, including `docs/setup.md`, and says
what each document is there to answer.

## Traps

- **One tool registry serves two surfaces.** `mcpTools` in [src/mcp/tools.ts](src/mcp/tools.ts)
  is spec 07's chat registry by reference plus `get_overview`, so a tool added or changed once is
  served to both the chat surface and the MCP server. Whoever misses this writes the change
  twice, and the second copy is the one that drifts.
- **The content policy applies per tool branch.** Every tool that answers with an item's own text
  calls `withholdsText` ([src/chat/tools/shared.ts](src/chat/tools/shared.ts)) and builds its own
  withheld answer: see the branches through [src/chat/tools/read.ts](src/chat/tools/read.ts)
  and [src/chat/tools/write.ts](src/chat/tools/write.ts). A field added to one branch and not the
  other makes the two content levels disagree, which is the class of bug spec 09 exists to
  prevent.
- **The running server serves `dist`, not the sources.** `npm start` runs
  `node dist/server/main.js`, and the SPA is served from `dist/web`. A green suite says nothing
  about the running instance until you rebuild.
- **`.github/copilot-instructions.md` is a copy of this file.** Most of Copilot reads a root
  `AGENTS.md` natively (the coding agent on github.com, Copilot code review, the cloud agent in the
  editors, the CLI), but Copilot Chat on every platform, and Visual Studio, read only
  `.github/copilot-instructions.md`. So that path holds a generated copy, written by
  [tools/docs/copilot-instructions.ts](tools/docs/copilot-instructions.ts) via
  `npm run docs:copilot`, and `test/docs/copilot-instructions.test.ts` fails when the copy and this
  file disagree. Editing this file means running that command in the same commit. It used to be a
  symlink, which reads correctly in a working tree and is served by the GitHub API as a blob holding
  the twelve bytes `../AGENTS.md`, so the surface most likely to be reading it got a filename.
- **Parts of docs/content-policy.md are generated.** Three blocks, each opened by an HTML
  comment naming `tools/docs/content-policy-examples.ts` and closed by an `end of the generated`
  one, come from the schema and the functions the classify job calls. Run
  `npm run docs:examples` rather than editing them by hand;
  `test/docs/content-policy-examples.test.ts` fails when the file and the module disagree.

## Tests before code

TDD, smallest useful red-green step, `npm run test:watch` running while you work. A change is
done when the relevant spec's acceptance criteria have tests asserting them, and the criterion
number is cited where the test asserts it.

## Checks before a commit

All of these, and the full suite rather than only the files you touched. It is what CI runs
([.github/workflows/ci.yml](.github/workflows/ci.yml)), in this order:

```sh
npm run lint        # eslint + prettier --check
npm run typecheck
npm test
npm run build
npm run build:site
```

`npm run build:site` renders the documents into the published site, so it is also the check that
every link between them still resolves. A link to a file the site does not publish fails the
build.

## Commits and pull requests

Commits are GPG-signed, always.

A commit produced with AI assistance carries a `Co-authored-by:` trailer naming the model that
did the work, for example `Co-authored-by: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>`. A
hand-written commit does not. The trailer is what makes the provenance of a change readable from
the history, so it is required rather than a formality. What has to be true is that it is there
and names the model: the history is not consistent about the capitalisation, so treat no one
spelling as canonical. Nothing else goes in, and in particular no "generated with" or
tool-advertisement line, of which the history has none.

No em-dashes anywhere written for a human audience: prose, code comments, commit messages, PR
bodies, docs. Use a colon, a comma, parentheses, or two sentences. Ordinary hyphens are fine.
`test/docs/no-em-dashes.test.ts` reads every tracked file and fails on one, so the rule is checked
rather than remembered. An en-dash marking a range is left alone, whether its ends are numbers
(`00–13`) or words (`start–end`).

A change reaches `main` through a branch and a pull request. CI has to be green and the change
reviewed before it merges, and it is squash-merged, so its subject line ends with its PR number.
Commits from before that settled read differently, in Conventional Commits style with a few
merge commits among them; follow the current convention rather than the older ones.

## Boundaries

Never commit `caroline.config.json`, `.env`, or anything under `data/` or `export/`: they hold
real credentials and real correspondence, and [.gitignore](.gitignore) already excludes them.

`.claude/` is git-ignored apart from `.claude/skills`, so a convention written there reaches
nobody else. Anything the team needs goes in a tracked file: this one, `docs/`, or a spec.
